sections.label: Assurance Package GST offsets
sections.summary: The Budget enhanced the Assurance Package by $640 million, committing that most Singaporean households will not feel the GST increase for at least five years.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: At this year's Budget, I enhanced the package by $640 million.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: With the Assurance Package, we had committed that the majority of Singaporean households will not feel the impact of the GST increase for at least five years and that lower-income households will not feel the impact for about 10 years.

sections.label: Assurance Package top-up to $8 billion
sections.summary: After reviewing elevated inflation, the Assurance Package is topped up by $1.4 billion to around $8 billion to meet committed offset levels.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The size of the Assurance Package will therefore need to be correspondingly increased to meet our committed levels of offsets.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Therefore, after reviewing the elevated inflation situation, I have decided to top up the Assurance Package by another $1.4 billion to reach around $8 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This ensures that the package continues to offset additional GST expenses for the majority of Singaporean households for at least five years, with around 10 years offset for lower-income households.

sections.label: GST impact on lower-income households
sections.summary: The bottom 10% of households pay no GST after permanent offsets, and the first three income deciles' effective GST rate stays below 3%.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: As I had explained in the Budget this year, on average, the bottom 10% of households do not pay any GST at all after the permanent offsets.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And even after the GST increase, the effective GST rate for households in the first three income deciles remains unchanged at below 3%.

sections.label: Tier 1 and Tier 2 offences
sections.summary: Tier 1 offences carry up to 10 years' imprisonment and/or a $500,000 fine; Tier 2 offences carry up to one year and/or a $50,000 fine.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Tier 1 offences carry a maximum imprisonment term of 10 years and/or maximum fine of $500,000.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This is a step up from the maximum imprisonment term of seven years for the offence of fraudulent trading, which such offenders are currently prosecuted under, and is intended to convey a strong deterrence message.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Tier 2 offences apply to current or former sole-proprietors, partners or directors of business entities that are used in Missing Trader Fraud schemes.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: These persons typically incorporate entities which are then used by syndicates for fraudulent purposes.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Tier 2 offences carry a maximum imprisonment term of one year and/or maximum fine of $50,000.

sections.label: Comptroller extending GST filing deadline
sections.summary: Clause 9 empowers the Comptroller of GST to extend the filing deadline for GST returns where necessary, such as during COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The last amendment, provided by clause 9, empowers the Comptroller of GST to extend the filing deadline for GST returns.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This allows the Comptroller the flexibility and authority to administer the GST regime efficiently, by extending the deadline for filing GST returns where necessary, such as during COVID-19.

sections.label: Diversified tax revenue sources
sections.summary: Corporate taxes, personal income taxes, GST and NIRC are among the Government's revenue sources, with NIRC the largest contributor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Every year the Government draws revenues from a diversified sources of taxes to pay for our current expenditures, with corporate taxes and personal income taxes among the top contributors, at 18.3% and 13.6% of total revenue respectively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The GST contributed 12.2% or $12.8 billion, our third largest revenue contributor; while the NIRC at 18.7% is now the largest revenue contributor to balance our Budget.

sections.label: Support packages and GST delay
sections.summary: The Government provided a $560 million Household Support Package, a $1.5 billion October package, and a $6.64 billion Assurance Package that delays the GST increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: This year I saw how the Government had made good on this commitment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We have a $560 million package, the Household Support Package, in the Budget 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: More recently, another $1.5 billion package in October to help Singaporeans to cope with the cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: To help with the GST increase, the Government has another set of support measures, which is the Assurance Package that was announced and has since been enlarged to $6.64 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The Assurance Package effectively delays the GST increase by five years for the majority and 10 years for the lower-income.

sections.label: GST increase in two steps
sections.summary: The Government will carry out the GST increase in two steps of 1% over two years, rather than one step of 2% this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The Government will carry out the GST increase in two steps: 1% over two years, rather than one step of 2% this year.

sections.label: Reducing retained NIRC to 40%
sections.summary: Based on Budget 2022 NIRC estimates of $21.5 billion, reducing the retained NIRC to 40% would mean more than $4 billion not going into past reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: To dive a little bit more, based on the Budget 2022 NIRC estimates of $21.5 billion, reducing the retained NIRC to 40% would mean more than $4 billion will not be going into past reserves for reinvesting.

sections.label: Government's diversified revenue approach
sections.summary: The speaker prefers the Government's approach of building diversified revenue with various taxes and NIRC to meet spending commitments and grow reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: I have also looked at the Workers' Party's current proposal which, like I said earlier, there are some aspects that I do not disagree.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: But when I look at all things in totality, I still prefer the Government's approach, which is that we continually build a diversified and stable source of revenue with income tax, corporate tax, wealth tax, property tax, GST and others, and augment with NIRC that we have to meet our current and longer-term spending commitments and continue to grow our reserves as they are our only backstop for our survivability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Growing our reserves will also help increase NIRC, which will reduce the overall tax burden, even as we plan to spend exponentially more in the future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: For a tiny country with no natural resources, we need an even higher factor of safety to navigate through the troubled and more uncertain world that we are in today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In the horizon ahead, we need this added strength, where we must be prepared for more and even bigger external shocks to come.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: This Parliament must be about doing the right thing and the right thing for us to do today is to secure our finances in a responsible way so that we can really take care and look after the different groups of Singaporeans – those who are growing older, the families who support them, the middle-income, the lower-income, the retirees, the young Singaporeans and the future generations.

sections.label: FY2021 operating revenues
sections.summary: Overall operating revenues were $82.5 billion for FY2021, $5.8 billion higher than Budget 2021 and $2.1 billion higher than the revised estimate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Overall operating revenues worked out to be $82.5 billion for FY2021 – $5.8 billion higher, compared to $76.6 billion as initially budgeted in Budget 2021 and $2.1 billion higher than the revised estimate of $80.4 billion as of Budget 2022.

sections.label: Primary deficit improvement
sections.summary: Combining higher revenues and lower expenses improved the Government's primary deficit by $5.7 billion, more than sufficient to cover the $1.5 billion support package.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Combining higher revenues and lower expenses would mean that the Government's primary deficit improved by $5.7 billion which, again, is more than sufficient to cover the recent $1.5 billion support package.

sections.label: Government operating revenue first half
sections.summary: Asks the Deputy Prime Minister how much better the fiscal position was in the first half and its projected year-end level.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I would thus like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister once again just how much better was our fiscal position in the first half of the year and what is this projected to be by the end of the financial year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I ask because, based on operating revenue data for the first half of the financial year, it appears that the total Government operating revenue of $48.9 billion is already about 60% of the full-year FY2022 estimates from Budget 2022.

sections.label: Core and headline inflation
sections.summary: Core inflation reached 5.3% and headline inflation 7.5%, the highest levels since 2008.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The current circumstances have proven otherwise, unfortunately, where core inflation and headline inflation have both accelerated over the course of the year, reaching 5.3% for core inflation and 7.5% for headline inflation – the highest levels since 14 years ago in 2008.

sections.label: Assistance packages cover cost increase
sections.summary: One-off assistance packages can cover just over half of the cost-of-living increase for middle-income households this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: If you consider the effects of the Household Support Package, public transport vouchers and the two cost-of-living packages in June and October, these arguably one-off assistance packages can cover just over half of the increase in cost of living for middle-income households on average this year.

sections.label: Household expenditure versus benefits
sections.summary: With 6% headline inflation, household expenditures rise about $2,500 yearly while the two cost-of-living packages give only $800 more in benefits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Even if we incorporate only the 6% headline inflation across both 2022 and 2023, household expenditures will increase by about $2,500 a year over those two years whereas the two sets of cost-of-living packages in June and October will only result in an $800 increase in benefits across the Household Utilities Credit, cost-of-living Special Payments and additional CDC vouchers that these households will qualify for.

sections.label: Assurance Package versus household expenditure
sections.summary: For a middle-income couple with two young children, the five-year Assurance Package totals $3,850 against estimated annual household expenditure of $40,320.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Back to the case of a middle-income couple with two young children, as illustrated by MOF, the total Assurance Package over five years amounts to $3,850, compared to the estimated annual household expenditure of $40,320.

sections.label: GST increase and NIR ceiling
sections.summary: The Workers' Party cannot support the Bill raising GST to 8% in 2023 and 9% from 2024, and asks about the 50% NIR ceiling.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Given that the core amendment in this Bill is to raise GST to 8% in 2023 and to 9% from 2024 onwards, the Workers' Party cannot support this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My clarification is really in relation to the 50% ceiling on the net investment returns (NIR) that goes into the Budget.

sections.label: Nothing cast in stone
sections.summary: The speaker states that nothing is cast in stone or forever.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: Well, Sir, nothing is cast in stone or is forever.

sections.label: Safeguarding finances and reserves
sections.summary: The speaker says finances should be safeguarded, reserves are a backstop, and the current balance is the best that can be struck.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: At this point in time, we should safeguard our finances as much as we can, always bear in mind that reserves are backstop that we want to be able to deal with situations, such as we have seen during the COVID-19 pandemic and we had to draw down $50 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: There could be other crises along the way that we will be required to take some actions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: So, there is no scientific rule about whether it is 50%:50%, or 40%:60%, but in my view, this is the best balance you can strike.

sections.label: Cost of living support packages
sections.summary: The Government extended cost-of-living support, including a $560 million Household Support Package, CDC vouchers, and two $1.5 billion packages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Second, the Government has extended substantial assistance for cost of living, in the form of support packages, beginning with the $560 million Household Support Package in Budget 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: It also brought forward some of the measures, like CDC vouchers in April 2022, and rolled out an additional $1.5 billion support package in June 2022 to provide immediate help for lower-income and more vulnerable groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Then, as recently as two weeks ago, the Government announced an additional $1.5 billion support package to provide further relief for all Singaporean households, including a cost-of-living special payment of up to $500 cash for 2.5 million adult Singaporeans.

sections.label: Support measures covering inflation increase
sections.summary: A MOF technical report says four rounds of 2022 support measures helped retirees and the bottom 40% cover over 100% of projected inflation spending increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: From MOF's technical report, dated October 2022, I know that four rounds of support measures in 2022 have already helped retirees and the bottom 40% of Singaporeans cover more than 100% of their projected increase in spending due to inflation.

sections.label: GSTV fund administrative expenses
sections.summary: The passage asks about cost drivers of GSTV fund administrative expenses, which were $10.7 million in FY2021/2022, $200,000 more than the previous FY.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: In addition, what are the cost drivers of the administrative expenses under the GSTV fund, which for FY2021/2022, amounted to $10.7 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: This was $200,000 more than the previous FY.

sections.label: GST increase revenue and tourism
sections.summary: The passage asks how much additional revenue the GST increase will raise, how much comes from foreigners, and projected tourism recovery levels.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: How much additional revenue are we expecting to raise from the GST increase and how much of that are expected to come from foreigners, like tourists, and what is the projected level of tourism recovery compared to pre-pandemic levels as of today, 1 January 2023 and 1 January 2024, both in tourist numbers and the economic value that would be generated as a result?

sections.label: GST Amendment Bill penalties
sections.summary: The GST (Amendment) Bill will codify plans to raise GST from 7% to 9% over two years, with enhanced maximum penalties of a $500,000 fine and/or 10 years imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: However, I understand that it is already a chargeable offence – six men were charged in 2021 in connection with Nagore Trading.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: So, are the amendments only to include enhanced maximum penalties of a $500,000 fine and/or 10 years imprisonment?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The GST (Amendment) Bill will codify into law the Government's plans to increase GST from the current rate of 7% to a rate of 9% over two years.

sections.label: Postponing GST on essentials
sections.summary: The speaker suggests a temporary postponement of GST on essential items, allowing additional exemptions in section 16 of the principal Act.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Today, I wish to suggest why a temporary postponement of GST on essential items, in effect allowing for additional exemptions in the amendments in section 16 of the principal Act, has much to merit serious consideration.

sections.label: Inflation rate doubling
sections.summary: Each time, the inflation rate would more or less double for up to a year thereafter.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Each time, the inflation rate would more or less double for up to a year thereafter.

sections.label: Utilities and electricity costs
sections.summary: The cost of utilities has jumped by more than 16%, with electricity shooting north of 26%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The cost of utilities has jumped by more than 16%, with electricity in particular, shooting north of 26%.

sections.label: Exempting essential goods from GST
sections.summary: The proposal is to temporarily exempt these categories of essential goods and services from the GST hike altogether.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To temporarily exempt these categories of essential goods and services from the GST hike altogether.

sections.label: Healthcare spending and MOH expenditure
sections.summary: MOF estimated healthcare spending for 2021 to 2025 would rise by 0.5 percentage points of GDP, but MOH expenditure for fiscal years 2020 and 2021 grew by 3.5% of GDP, from 2.2%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: MOF had previously estimated that healthcare spending for the current five-year period between 2021 and 2025 was expected to increase by 0.5 percentage points of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As it turns out, total expenditure by MOH for fiscal years 2020 and 2021 busted this budget – it grew by 3.5% of GDP, from 2.2% – which is little surprise, given COVID-19 related expenditures.

sections.label: GST increase revenue size
sections.summary: A two-percentage point GST increase is expected to raise $3.5 billion, about 0.7% of current-day GDP, exceeding MOH's projected needs.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: After all, the $3.5 billion that a two-percentage point GST increase is expected to raise will amount to about 0.7% of current-day GDP, which is far greater than the projected increases needed by MOH for the couple of years ahead.

sections.label: Property tax revenue estimate
sections.summary: The speaker estimates property tax regime changes would raise about $0.4 billion, which is still insufficient.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In our own calculations, we estimate that the amounts raised by changes in the property tax regime would raise a non-trivial amount of about $0.4 billion, but this is still insufficient.

sections.label: Land sales revenue treatment
sections.summary: Using the Government's treatment of land leases under 10 years and taking the full 10-year amount would raise over $2 billion.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Rather, as we have explained we are using the Government's own treatment of land leases with tenure of less than 10 years, which currently gets directed to recurring revenues, and, instead, we are saying "Let's take this, be consistent and take the full amount of the 10 years, whether the tenure of the land sales is for 30 years or 60 years or 99 years, and instead take that amount and put that into our recurrent revenue".

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This will raise in excess of $2 billion which is a big part of where this revenue strategy would raise necessary funds.

sections.label: NIRC contribution adjustment
sections.summary: The speaker calculated that the Government's 2008 NIRC contribution adjustment moved from about 10% to the current 50%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Based on our calculations, we calculated that when the Government adjusted its NIRC contribution in 2008, it moved from about a contribution of 10% to the current 50%.

sections.label: GST revenue and rebates
sections.summary: GST revenue will be higher next year even without a rate increase, and announced packages amount to less than the $8 billion excess revenue.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Similarly, GST revenue will automatically be higher in dollar terms next year – even if it does not increase from the current rate of 7% – because GST will be levied on the higher sticker prices already being charged for goods and services.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is why I had stressed, in my earlier speeches, that the Government has a responsibility to rebate fiscal surpluses that has resulted from inflation —

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: And the Government has announced two and now recently three packages which amount to – still in our calculations – less than the $8 billion excess revenue that had been raised in the most recent fiscal year.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: So, Mr Speaker, for reasons outlined in this speech and earlier ones, I cannot support the increase in GST.

sections.label: Cost of living support
sections.summary: The Labour Movement is thankful for the 22 October $1.5 billion cost of living support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The Labour Movement is thankful for the 22 October $1.5 billion cost of living support.

sections.label: Assurance Package GST support
sections.summary: The Assurance Package will support workers when GST increases next year, boosted from $6.6 billion to $8 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: We are also mindful that the Assurance Package will still be in place to support workers when GST kicks in next year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: It was $6.6 billion; it will be boosted to $8 billion.

sections.label: CTCs Operation Technology Roadmap
sections.summary: By end of 2025, 2,500 CTCs will develop the Operation and Technology Roadmap programme with companies in partnership with the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: This was done in partnership with the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: These 2,500 CTCs, by the end of 2025, will develop the Operation and Technology Roadmap programme (OTR) with companies.

sections.label: Retail sector wage increase
sections.summary: It has served economic and social purposes, expanded to the retail sector, and workers will see around 8.5% wage increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: It has served both economic and social purposes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: We have expanded to the retail sector and workers will see around 8.5% wage increase.

sections.label: Real basic wage growth
sections.summary: Real basic wages grew by 2.8% a year over the last 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: For example, real basic wages grew by 2.8% a year over the last 10 years.

sections.label: NTUC Enterprise support packages
sections.summary: NTUC Enterprise rolled out $50 million in 2020 and $20 million in 2021, and NTUC launched a $3.7 million programme in August for 28,000 lower-wage workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: In recent years, when the pandemic first hit in 2020, NTUC Enterprise rolled out a $50 million support package to help with the cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: In 2021, they rolled out another $20 million package to manage the cost of living and help stretch savings across different areas such as insurance, healthcare, education, and financial planning.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: This year, NTUC also launched a $3.7 million NTUC Care Fund (Special assistance) Programme in August to help 28,000 lower-wage income workers defray daily expenses and higher inflation.

sections.label: FairPrice GST discount items
sections.summary: Ahead of the GST increase, NTUC FairPrice will offer a discount on 500 essential items for the first six months of 2023.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Ahead of the implementation of Goods and Services Tax (GST) increase, NTUC FairPrice has announced that it will be offering a discount on 500 essential items for the first six months of 2023.

sections.label: PSP GST hike opposition
sections.summary: Francis Yuen of the Progress Singapore Party called the GST hike unnecessary, untimely and uncompassionate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As the Progress Singapore Party's Secretary-General Francis Yuen has said, the move to hike GST is unnecessary, untimely and uncompassionate.

sections.label: Sandwich class GST cost
sections.summary: The speaker said the sandwich class would pay $1.2 billion more from the full 2% GST hike amid inflation and housing prices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In my speech during the Committee of Supply Debate in February, I have stated that the sandwich class would be paying $1.2 billion more as a result of the full implementation of the 2% GST hike at a time when they are facing challenges with soaring inflation and escalating housing prices.

sections.label: PSP does not support Bill
sections.summary: The Progress Singapore Party does not support the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: (In English) Mr Speaker, Sir, the Progress Singapore Party does not support the Bill.

sections.label: Ah Gong tax returns
sections.summary: Ah Gong said for every dollar collected from Ah Seng, $2 or $3 was given back per tax dollar.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: In fact, Ah Gong has repeatedly mentioned that for every dollar that he collected from Ah Seng to plan for this future and future generations, he would have collected, collectively, from others and given back to Ah Seng $2 for every dollar of tax that he has paid or in fact, $3 for every single tax dollar.

sections.label: MAS 2022 inflation forecasts
sections.summary: MAS expects 2022 headline inflation of 5% to 6% and core inflation averaging 3% to 4%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: MAS expects headline inflation in 2022 to come between 5% and 6%, with core inflation to average between 3% and 4%.

sections.label: MTI GDP growth forecast
sections.summary: MTI narrowed Singapore's 2022 GDP growth range to 3% to 4% from 3% to 5%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: MTI narrowed its range for Singapore's GDP growth this year to 3% to 4% from an earlier projection of 3% to 5%.

sections.label: Healthcare spending growth projection
sections.summary: DPM Wong said healthcare spending nearly tripled from $3.7 billion in 2010 to $11.3 billion in 2019, and could reach around $27 billion by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In the last Budget debate in February this year, Deputy Prime Minister Wong highlighted that we almost tripled healthcare spending from $3.7 billion in 2010 to $11.3 billion in 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: If our current healthcare spending continues to increase at a similar rate over the coming decade, we will spend around $27 billion by 2030.

sections.label: Global minimum effective tax rate
sections.summary: Pillar Two of the multilateral consensus includes a global minimum effective tax rate of 15%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Pillar Two of the multilateral consensus includes a global minimum effective tax rate of 15%.

sections.label: Spending on workforce and research
sections.summary: More spending is needed on workforce programmes and research collaborations, including a $65 million Joint Lab programme with A-star, Rolls-Royce and SAESL.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: At the very least, we will have to spend more on our workforce through programmes like career conversion programmes to train, upskill and attract more of our local talents into high growth industries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We also have to spend more to form collaborations with research institutions like the $65 million Joint Lab programmes between A-star, Rolls-Royce and Singapore Aero Engine Services Private Limited (SAESL) to drive productivity and develop novel technologies for the world.

sections.label: GST income sources
sections.summary: Sixty percent of GST income comes from the top 20% income earners and foreigners spending in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Sixty percent of GST income comes from the top 20% income earners and foreigners spending in Singapore.

sections.label: Pre-COVID tourist arrivals and spending
sections.summary: STAN data shows 22.84 million tourists visited Singapore in 2019 and spent an average of more than $1,000 per stay.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: According to the Singapore Tourism Analytics Network (STAN), 22.84 million tourists visited Singapore in pre-COVID-19 2019 and spent an average of more than $1,000 during their stay.

sections.label: GST Vouchers offset effect
sections.summary: With 9% GST and enhanced GST Vouchers, 70% of the population pays less than the current 7% GST, and the bottom 10% of households pay no GST after the offset.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In fact, with the 9% GST and enhanced GST Vouchers, 70% of the population will pay less than the current 7% GST and the bottom 10% of Singapore households, including many retiree households, do not pay GST at all after the offset.

sections.label: Healthcare expenditure growth
sections.summary: Healthcare expenditure rose from about $3 billion to $10 billion a year between 2012 and 2022, and is expected to reach $27 billion a year by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Between 2012 and 2022, healthcare expenditure has increased from around $3 billion to $10 billion a year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In fact, this amount will continue to increase and is expected to reach $27 billion a year by 2030.

sections.label: Assurance Package cash payouts
sections.summary: The Assurance Package gives all adult Singaporeans cash payouts of $700 to $1,600 over five years, offsetting GST spending for most households.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: In addition, the Assurance Package means that all adult Singaporeans will receive cash payouts between $700 and $1,600 over five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: This can offset at least five years’ worth of additional GST spending for most households, and 10 years for those living in 1-room to 3-room HDB flats.

sections.label: GST collected from top households
sections.summary: The top 20% of households, foreigners and tourists account for more than 60% of GST collected.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: As data from previous years show, the top 20% of the households here, foreigners and tourists account for more than 60% of the GST collected.

sections.label: Dialysis cost and Mdm L's income
sections.summary: Dialysis costs about $300 per month after subsidy, and Mdm L earns about $2,800 a month as a childcare teacher.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The dialysis cost is about $300 per month after subsidy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The family was relieved that Mdm L could continue working and she currently earns about $2,800 a month as a childcare teacher.

sections.label: MediSave withdrawal limits request
sections.summary: Citing rising medical costs and an ageing population needing more support, the speaker asks for higher MediSave withdrawal limits.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: In view of rising medical costs and that one of the key reasons why we have to increase GST is that our ageing population requires more support, I would also like to ask for higher withdrawal limits for MediSave.

sections.label: Workers' Party GST alternatives
sections.summary: The Workers' Party proposed alternatives to the GST hike: more NIRC use, land sales as operating revenue, 15% corporate tax, and higher sin taxes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party has proposed the following as alternatives to the GST hike: (a) to use more of the net investment returns contribution, or NIRC, for expenditure, that is, 60% instead of the current 50%, and to put back a smaller amount, 40%, into the reserves; (b) to use a portion of our land sales as operating revenue; (c) raising corporate tax so that the effective tax rate is 15%; (d) raising tax on activities which have negative externalities and raising "sin" tax.

sections.label: Generational cost of public services
sections.summary: Each generation must, as far as possible, bear the cost of the public services it consumes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: The first principle in terms of taxes and expenditure is that each generation must, as far as possible, bear the cost of the public services it consumes.

sections.label: NIRC split between generations
sections.summary: The current generation takes 50% of the NIRC and leaves 50% for the next generation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: One can see many examples of this around the world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: This current generation takes 50% of the NIRC and leaves 50% for the next generation.

sections.label: No over-saving for Singapore
sections.summary: For a small country like Singapore, there is no such thing as over-saving.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: For a small country like Singapore, there is no such thing as over-saving.

sections.label: Targeted assistance for severe pain
sections.summary: Where the pain is most severe and sharpest, the most pain relief will be given through targeted assistance schemes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Where the pain is most severe and sharpest, we will give the most pain relief through targeted assistance schemes.

sections.label: Hike and prudent consumption
sections.summary: The hike reminds the Government and the individual to remain prudent in consumption behaviour amid tough economic times.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: That is how Singapore can continue to stay resilient, thrive and prosper.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: But at a deeper level, the hike reminds us, both the Government and the individual, that we need to remain prudent in our consumption behaviour and that the world is going through tough economic times.

sections.label: Buffering Singaporeans from GST hike
sections.summary: Even with the impending GST hike, the Assurance Package and Enhanced GSTV scheme effectively buffer many Singaporeans from the increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Even with the impending GST hike, the Assurance Package and Enhanced GSTV scheme effectively buffer many Singaporeans from the increase.

sections.label: Long-term planning versus analgesia
sections.summary: Planning for long-term resilience and supporting Singaporeans today is better than providing analgesia to numb the senses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Planning for the long-term interest of successive generations of Singaporeans, always ensuring that Singapore remains resilient through choppy waters, while at the same time, supporting Singaporeans in facing the challenges of today, is surely a better, more holistic approach than providing analgesia to numb the senses so that we can all pretend that the pain does not exist.

sections.label: NIRC contribution rate increase
sections.summary: Calculations suggest the NIRC contribution rose from about 10% or 20% to the present 50%.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: Our own calculations suggest that it went from somewhere in the order of 10% or 20% of the NIRC contribution up to the present rate of 50%.

sections.label: NIRC 50-50 split
sections.summary: The Workers' Party and the speaker agree on the NIRC system, and the speaker thinks 50-50 is about right.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: As far as I know, the Workers' Party agrees with having the NIRC system and so do I.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: But the question that they have posed is should we have 50-50 or should we allow 60% to be used as expenditure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: For now, I think 50-50 is about right.

sections.label: Tapping reserves with President's permission
sections.summary: If using 50% of NIRC is not enough, the Government can tap reserves with the President's permission.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: If using 50% of NIRC is not enough, there is a mechanism for the Government to tap on the reserves, with the permission of the President.

sections.label: Assurance Package offsets GST increase
sections.summary: The Assurance Package means most Singaporean households will not feel the GST increase for at least five years, and lower-income families for about 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: While none of us likes an increase in GST, it is reassuring to know that with the Assurance Package, the majority of Singaporean households will not feel the impact of the GST increase for at least five years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: For lower-income families, the Assurance Package will delay the impact of the GST increase by about 10 years.

sections.label: Assurance Package cash payouts
sections.summary: Every adult Singaporean aged 21 and above will get $700 to $1,600 over five years from December this year to 2026 to offset GST expenses.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: What this means is that with the cash payout of the Assurance Package, every adult Singaporean aged 21 and above, depending on assessable annual income and home ownership, will get a total cash payout of between $700 and $1,600 over five years from December this year to 2026 to offset the additional GST expenses.

sections.label: GST offset cash payout
sections.summary: A $700 payout over five years means $140 yearly, offsetting 2% of the GST increase for those spending $580 monthly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: What it means, really, is, if someone falls into the category of getting $700 over the five years, what it means is that, for each year, that person will receive a $140 offset.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: That means that $140 a year will offset 2% of the GST increase over the five years, which, effectively, means that for a spending of $580 a month for each individual – this is just the cash payout component	– you will not be paying GST.

sections.label: Sandwich generation rising costs
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the Government reviews relief for the sandwich generation, as businesses and consumers bear GST-driven cost increases.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: So, I hope that the Government will also continue to review and provide relevant relief in areas that can help the sandwich generation manage rising cost.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: We can expect that businesses, too, will be impacted by the increase in GST and will, inevitably, increase the cost of their products and services; and the consumer will, ultimately, bear the cost increase.

sections.label: GST increase with reliefs
sections.summary: Taken with the Assurance Package and other reliefs, the GST increase is delayed and, for lower-income, completely removed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Effectively, if we look at not just the GST increase on its own, but the GST increase together with the other reliefs – both the Assurance Package as well as the cost of living and all the other packages – taken in totality, it does, in fact, delay and, in some cases, actually, for the lower-income, completely remove the impact of the GST increase.

sections.label: AV eligibility and economy
sections.summary: The speaker asks to review AV eligibility criteria for support schemes while keeping the economy strong and providing quality jobs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: With rising prices and higher cost of living, I ask that we review and calibrate the AV eligibility criterion for appropriate support schemes for these segments.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: All said and done, while we are debating the need to increase GST and to provide support for those who need support, let us not lose focus on the need to continue to keep our economy strong and to provide quality jobs for Singaporeans.

sections.label: Healthcare costs and seniors
sections.summary: Government healthcare provision gives seniors peace of mind, while healthcare costs more than tripled and are projected to reach $59 billion in 2030.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: This step change I have seen that the Government has provided in healthcare provision affords great peace of mind to our seniors and their families and greatly reduces their financial burden.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: I must acknowledge that during this same period, we have seen healthcare costs more than triple and, given our rapidly ageing population, is projected to reach $59 billion in 2030 from $22 billion in 2018.

sections.label: Reserves contributions doubled
sections.summary: Contributions from reserves to fund public expenditures doubled in 10 years, from about $8 billion in 2011 to $20 billion in 2021.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Contributions from our reserves to fund public expenditures has already doubled in 10 years, ballooning from about $8 billion in 2011 to $20 billion in 2021.

sections.label: Reserves used for COVID-19
sections.summary: Reserves served as a war chest, with about $37 billion drawn to fight COVID-19 and unlikely to be replaced soon.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Our reserves also served as a precious war chest that saw us through the crisis of a generation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: We drew about $37 billion to fight the COVID-19 pandemic, and we are unlikely to be able to put back what we have drawn down, anytime soon.

sections.label: Household support cost-of-living packages
sections.summary: Government made good on its commitment with successive household support packages, including $1.5 billion in October, totalling $3.5 billion this year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: And also, in response to our numerous queries on support for cost of living, the Government has consistently responded that it would do more should the need arise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: I am therefore, reassured to see the Government make good on this commitment with the successive rounds of household support packages, including the latest $1.5 billion announced in October, adding up to a total of $3.5 billion this year alone.

sections.label: Support schemes and funding concerns
sections.summary: Beneficiaries struggle to understand varied support schemes, and the Government is called to monitor profiteering and address funding for healthcare and social expenditures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Currently, not all eligible beneficiaries can understand how the slew of support schemes will benefit them, as they vary in eligibility cut-offs, payment modes, flat type, household size and so on.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: So, I would to call on the Government to monitor this space closely, through the Committee Against Profiteering and to check inflation fuelled by opportunistic price increases.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: We have a long list of deserving initiatives that warrant Government funding, especially those towards supporting our healthcare and social expenditures to take care of our seniors and retirees, given our rapidly ageing society.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: We must, with courage and wisdom, confront the question of how to pay for them today, whilst safeguarding Singapore's tomorrow.

sections.label: Progressive Wage Model expansion
sections.summary: The Union backs the Progressive Wage Model's rollout in cleaning, security, landscape, retail and food services, and notes the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We can choose to look on and rue rising prices like sitting ducks or match the rising cost of living with increased productivity and fortified wages undergirded by the equitable and sustainable gains sharing.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: That is exactly why the Union has thrown its weight behind the rollout and expansion of the Progressive Wage Model, deepening its reach in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors, as well as being newly implemented in the retail sector in September this year, with the Food Services sector following very closely in six months' time and more sectors to come in the months ahead.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: We are encouraged by the Government’s commitment to resilience-building on top of mere relief-provisions as seen in the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) introduced during Budget 2022.

sections.label: Support for older workers
sections.summary: Fears of nest eggs eroding after productive years prompt a call for continued Government grants and funding support for older workers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: These concerns are exacerbated, especially after their productive years, with fears rising of nest eggs being eroded by the rising costs of living, and, indeed, the aftermath of COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Therefore, I call on the Government to strengthen and continue support for our older workers through grants and other funding support.

sections.label: Non-GST-registered small businesses
sections.summary: Many small businesses are not GST-registered, so they cannot charge GST and claim GST costs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Many of these small businesses, Mr Speaker, also happen to be not GST-registered, meaning that they are unable to charge GST and claim GST costs.

sections.label: Support for drivers' rising costs
sections.summary: Asks what more can be done for drivers facing rising costs, suggesting extending an allowance to low-value goods and resetting it annually.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Our drivers, being price takers, and individually not earning enough to be GST-registered, what more can we do to cushion the impact of rising costs handed down to them from upstream stakeholders?

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: While short-term measures, such as support vouchers, are welcomed, what other policy levers can we pull for the longer term?

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Perhaps this allowance can be extended to a basket of low-value goods and can be considered and reset on an annual basis.

sections.label: Fair revenue raising for society
sections.summary: States that ensuring a fair system of raising revenue is a responsible way of easing the burden on younger workers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: (In English): Ensuring a fair system of raising revenue to meet our society’s needs is a responsible way of easing the burden of our younger generation of workers who have to support a larger population of older residents in the years to come.

sections.label: Offence of fraudulent arrangements
sections.summary: Under new section 62C, participating in a specified arrangement knowing it is for a fraudulent purpose is an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under the new section 62C, it is an offence to participate in a specified arrangement knowing that it is for a fraudulent purpose.

sections.label: Strict liability for missing trader fraud
sections.summary: Section 62C makes a sole proprietor, partner or director strictly liable if their entity is used to commit missing trader fraud.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Section 62C also makes a sole proprietor, partner or director strictly liable if their entity is used to commit missing trader fraud.

sections.label: Deciding which offence to proceed on
sections.summary: Asks what the Ministry will consider in deciding which offence to proceed on, noting the participation offence's penalties are 10 times higher.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister explain what the Ministry will consider in deciding which offence to proceed on?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This is significant because the maximum fine and prison term for participation is 10 times as much as that for the strict-liability offence.

sections.label: CAP 2007 feedback and single case
sections.summary: When CAP last convened in 2007, it received 200 pieces of feedback and made public only a single case, a childcare centre.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The last time that CAP convened in 2007, it received 200 pieces of feedback and ended up making public only a single case – a childcare centre.

sections.label: Financial pandemic and Jobs Credit
sections.summary: The 2009 Global Financial Crisis saw $4.5 billion Jobs Credit Scheme and skills upgrading to protect lives and livelihoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Much has been said of our fight with the COVID-19 pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It was a similar case with the financial pandemic in 2009 during the Global Financial Crisis where we were able to muster financial resources to protect lives and livelihoods through the $4.5 billion Jobs Credit Scheme and skills upgrading programme.

sections.label: Effective GST rates by income
sections.summary: Lower-income and retirees pay effective GST of zero to 3%, middle segment around four to 7%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In the prospective regime, the lower-income, including retirees, continue to pay an effective GST rate of zero to 3%, the middle segment or those with per capita household income from $2,000 to $4,000 will pay around four to 7%, of which 7% is already the existing GST rate.

sections.label: Cost of Living packages
sections.summary: Government responded to inflation with two $1.5 billion Cost of Living packages announced in June and October.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Relating to the high inflation and the cost of living, I am heartened that the Government has responded decisively in addressing cost of living concerns, with two $1.5 billion Cost of Living packages that were first announced in June and then in October this year, which is on top of the Household Support Package.

sections.label: Support for smaller SMEs
sections.summary: Question asks if there will be further support for smaller SMEs to navigate the GST rate change.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Against this, can the Deputy Prime Minister share if there will be further support for smaller SMEs to better navigate the GST rate change?

sections.label: Actual GST paid by income
sections.summary: With Assurance Package and GST Vouchers, low-income and retirees pay 0% to 3%, middle-income 4% to 7%, high-income 7% to 9%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: If we include the GST and the various assistance packages such as the $6.6 billion Assurance Package and the annual GST Vouchers, it is estimated that the actual GST paid by the low-income and retirees is between 0% to 3% and that for the middle-income is 4% to 7%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Only those high-income earners will have to pay 7% to 9% GST.

sections.label: Assistance Packages and Assurance Package
sections.summary: Two Assistance Packages announced in June and October help with rising cost of living, and updated Assurance Package will be announced next year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For example, the two additional Assistance Packages announced in June and October this year will help Singaporeans cope with the rising cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Deputy Prime Minister has also just announced that the Government will announce the updated Assurance Package next year.

sections.label: Ah Seng tax benefits
sections.summary: Lower-income Ah Seng receives $4 in benefits per dollar of tax, middle-income $2, with half of investment returns spent on him.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
sentences.text: As my Parliament colleague Mr Shawn Huang mentioned just now, if Ah Seng is from the lower-income group, for every one dollar of tax that he pays to Ah Gong, he will receive $4 in benefits.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
sentences.text: If Ah Seng is middle-income, every dollar that he pays to Ah Gong, he will receive $2 in benefits.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
sentences.text: In fact, part of Ah Seng’s expenditure every year comes from the returns of the invested savings that Ah Gong and Ah Ma have accumulated. 50% of the returns are spent on Ah Seng and his family, while the other half is put back into the savings, so that the savings can grow and achieve more returns in future.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
sentences.text: For every $5 Ah Seng needs every year, $1 comes from the 50% of the returns of Ah Gong's investment.

sections.label: Global value added tax rates
sections.summary: Sweden, the UK and Japan use value added taxes at higher rates than Singapore: 25%, 20% and 10%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Globally, such value added taxes have been used at higher rates than Singapore – Sweden at 25%, UK at 20% and Japan at 10%.

sections.label: Income tax rate history
sections.summary: Corporate and personal income tax fell from 40% before 1985 to 24% personal and 17% corporate now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Historically, the rate of corporate and personal income taxes was at 40% before 1985; this came down to 33% after the recession in 1985.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: After GST was enacted, it came down further, to 28%, now it is up to 24% for personal income tax and 17% for corporate tax.

sections.label: Staggered GST increase 2003-2004
sections.summary: The Government staggered the GST increase by 1% in 2003 and 1% in 2004.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Government decided to stagger the GST increase much like this time; 1% in 2003 and 1% in 2004.

sections.label: GST hike to 7%
sections.summary: After the GST hike, fiscal discipline, positive growth and improved livelihoods resulted, and Tharman Shanmugaratnam announced the GST hike to 7%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As a result of the GST hike, we kept fiscal discipline, turned in positive economic growth and improved the livelihoods of Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: That year, Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, as he then was, announced the GST hike to 7%.

sections.label: GST Voucher scheme permanence
sections.summary: In 2012, the GST Voucher scheme was made permanent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In 2012, the GST Voucher scheme was made permanent.

sections.label: GST increase support
sections.summary: The speaker supports the GST increase with features and schemes to help the less well-off, saying further tax base increases would upset the balance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: To further increase these tax bases will upset this balance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I therefore support the increase in GST with the features and schemes addressed to help the less well-off.

sections.label: 50-50 NIRC ratio
sections.summary: The 50-50 NIRC ratio is equitable because it balances current needs with future needs on an equal platform.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The 50-50 NIRC ratio is equitable because it balances current needs with future needs, putting it on an equal platform.

sections.label: Cost-of-living allocation
sections.summary: $3.5 billion has been allocated for Singaporeans for cost-of-living issues alone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For cost-of-living issues alone, $3.5 billion has been allocated for Singaporeans.

sections.label: WP and GST hike
sections.summary: WP's 2020 call led to the Public Defenders Act, but WP dismisses the GST hike as unnecessary or bad timing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: One vivid example is WP's call to level the playing field for accused persons in 2020, which led to the passing of the Public Defenders Act this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: On the other hand, what we see as true political courage in the context of a GST hike, the WP dismisses as being unnecessary or bad timing.

sections.label: Voluntary GST registration
sections.summary: Seven in 10 businesses newly registering for GST already do so voluntarily.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Today, seven in 10 businesses that newly register for GST already do so voluntarily.

sections.label: Missing Trader Fraud prosecution
sections.summary: Section 62C introduces a two-tiered approach to prosecute Missing Trader Fraud offenders based on culpability with enhanced penalties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Currently, perpetrators of Missing Trader Fraud can only be prosecuted under non-tax Acts like the Companies Act, but as I mentioned just now, these provisions may not be able to cater to the specificities of Missing Trader Fraud, which is a very complex tax crime.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Therefore, section 62C addresses this by introducing a new two-tiered approach to prosecute offenders based on their level of culpability and through enhanced penalties.

sections.label: Inflation support for households
sections.summary: Three packages totalling over $3.5 billion offset inflation-driven spending increases for lower-income and retiree households, and over half for middle-income households.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Both globally and in Singapore, the "new normal" may well be a higher rate of inflation than what we were used to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why where inflation is concerned, the Government has extended comprehensive support to Singaporeans, especially lower- and middle-income families, through three packages this year totalling more than $3.5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On average, as I have explained, these measures will fully offset the inflation-driven increases in spending for lower-income and retiree households – fully offset the increase in spending for lower-income and retiree households due to inflation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: For the typical middle-income household, the Government support provided will offset more than half of the inflation-driven increases in cost of living this year.

sections.label: Rising healthcare spending
sections.summary: Government healthcare spending tripled from $3.7 billion in FY2010 to $11.3 billion in FY2019 and is expected to rise from 2.2% to 3.5% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Government support and spending on healthcare has been rising over the past decade, tripling from $3.7 billion in FY2010 to $11.3 billion in FY2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Since then, we have continued to age, and our healthcare needs have become only more acute.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I have said this before, we expect the Government's healthcare spending to go up, from 2.2% of GDP to 3.5% of GDP.

sections.label: Workfare and Progressive Wage spending
sections.summary: Over $9 billion will be spent in the next five years on enhanced Workfare and the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, with further enhancements announced this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Mr Desmond Choo and Ms Yeo Wan Ling spoke passionately about this, and I assure them this is also a key priority for the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: This is why I had announced in the Budget that we will be spending over $9 billion over the next five years, on the enhanced Workfare and the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, and I announced further enhancements to the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme earlier this year.

sections.label: GST increase not delayed
sections.summary: The Government decided the GST increase could not be delayed further because the spending gap would otherwise snowball and leave programmes unfunded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: If we do not deal with this huge spending gap now and decisively, the problem will only snowball and very soon we will ourselves be unable to fund programmes that Singaporeans need.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why, having considered this so carefully before the Budget and after the Budget, even in the last few months when the global economic environment had deteriorated, we felt that there was no possibility for us to delay the GST increase any further.

sections.label: Second GST increase step
sections.summary: The second step of the increase in 2024 will proceed barring a severe global downturn, with a review if downside risks materialise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: If indeed such downside risks were to materialise and our economy is severely impacted, we will need to take a careful review and we will consider whether to proceed with the second step of the increase in 2024.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Barring a severe downturn in global economic circumstances, we will proceed with the second step of the increase to put our public finances on a much stronger footing and we will ensure that households are well-supported through the transition.

sections.label: FY2021 budget surplus
sections.summary: In FY2021, higher than expected revenue produced a surplus of $1.9 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In FY2021, we did enjoy higher than expected revenue and we had a surplus of $1.9 billion in FY2021.

sections.label: Lower NIRC and spending
sections.summary: The Government will accept lower NIRC and adjust spending or find other revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Given the trends that we expect over the coming years, it may well be that the expected long-term returns will have to come down – just based on these professional inputs and the assessment of these structural challenges we face.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And if so, the right approach and certainly the approach that the Government will take, is to accept the lower NIRC and either adjust our spending accordingly or we will have to find other forms of revenue.

sections.label: GST single-rate systems
sections.summary: 80% of countries introducing GST after 1995 chose a single-rate system like Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, according to the BBC report I read, 80% of countries which introduced GST after 1995, have opted for a single-rate system – like us, for good reason.

sections.label: Personal income tax rates
sections.summary: Loading all GST revenue on top personal income tax rates would raise them from 22% to 42%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Personal income tax – we have raised it in the Budget but if you want to raise more – for example, as I mentioned in the Budget debate – if you want to load all of the GST revenue on personal income tax and push it only for the top marginal rates, the top marginal rates will go up from 22% to 42%.

sections.label: Global minimum corporate tax
sections.summary: Pillar Two concerns a global minimum corporate tax of 15%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Pillar Two is where you talk about minimum corporate tax globally of 15%.

sections.label: Jobs and investments risk
sections.summary: Jobs and investments will be at risk if Singapore cannot offer equally attractive value propositions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Surely, our jobs and investments will be at risk if we are not able to keep pace and offer equally attractive value propositions in Singapore.

sections.label: GST and healthcare funding gap
sections.summary: GST revenues alone cannot meet the healthcare funding gap of 1.3 percentage points of GDP by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, as I said just now, the GST revenues alone are not even enough to meet our healthcare funding gap – 1.3 percentage points of GDP is the gap by 2030 but our GST increase only yields 0.7% of GDP.

sections.label: Fiscal gap management approach
sections.summary: The Government says it carefully considered every option and chose the best way to manage the fiscal gap and keep Singapore's fiscal foundation strong.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And I wonder if this is because they feel that this approach is the best way to advance their political agenda as they have been over the years – to paint the PAP Government as uncaring and out of touch.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have looked at each and every option very carefully and we have decided this is the best way to manage the fiscal gap that we face and make sure that we continue to keep Singapore's fiscal foundation strong and resilient, especially for the future.

sections.label: Cash payouts to unbanked
sections.summary: Most eligible Singaporeans receive cash payouts via PayNow or bank crediting, while unbanked recipients are now paid through GovCash instead of cheques.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Most eligible Singaporeans – about 98% of recipients – today get their cash payouts seamlessly through PayNow or direct bank crediting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Those who remain unbanked were previously paid via cheques which required encashment over bank counters, but we have since moved to using GovCash to make payments to these individuals and we expect the move to help reduce administrative costs and allow the unbanked to receive their payouts more quickly and conveniently.

sections.label: Committee feedback on GST misrepresentation
sections.summary: The Committee received around 140 feedback submissions between April and October, seven involving specific allegations of GST misrepresentation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The Committee received around 140 feedback submissions between April and October this year, of which seven involved specific allegations of GST misrepresentation.

sections.label: CAP monitoring and enforcement
sections.summary: CAP will continue to monitor closely and is prepared to publicly name egregious businesses and take enforcement actions promptly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: CAP will continue to monitor this closely, and they will be prepared to publicly name egregious businesses, and to take enforcement actions promptly.

sections.label: Timing of GST increase
sections.summary: Although the rate rises in 2023 and 2024, most Singaporean households will only start paying more GST nearer the end of this decade or later.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Although we are raising the rate in 2023 and 2024, the majority of Singaporean households will only start to pay more GST nearer the end of this decade or even later.

sections.label: Assurance Package offsetting GST
sections.summary: With the Assurance Package, most Singaporean households can offset at least five years of additional GST expenditure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: With the help of the Assurance Package, the majority of Singaporean households will be able to offset at least five years of additional GST expenditure.

sections.label: GST impact on bottom households
sections.summary: After Government support, the bottom 10% of households on average pay no GST at all.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, on average, after Government support, the bottom 10% of households do not have to pay any GST at all.

sections.label: Who bears GST
sections.summary: GST will be borne mainly by higher-income households, tourists and foreigners in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, GST will be borne mainly by higher-income households, tourists and foreigners in Singapore.

sections.label: FY2022 surplus and NIRC
sections.summary: FY2021 surplus and better-than-expected 2022 first-half outturn are fully used; no FY2022 surplus is expected, and NIRC should keep pace with economic growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: As I said just now, overall, the surplus in FY2021 and the better-than-expected outturn – revenue, net of expenditure – in the first half of 2022 have already been fully utilised for the packages this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Yes, there may well be some buoyant revenue sources.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But our spending is also going to be higher in the second half and, net-net overall, as I mentioned just now, we do not expect a surplus in FY2022 at the end of the financial year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On NIRC, I have also explained our position on NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I have said that, going forward, we anticipate that NIRC, which contributes about 3.5% of GDP to our revenue today, we think that is likely, over the longer term, to keep pace with economic growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: NIRC will keep pace with economic growth, we think, but this has not taken into consideration the potential for our expected long-term real rate of return to be reduced because of all these structural challenges that we have just been talking about – climate change, ageing population, geopolitical tensions.

sections.label: Pausing second GST step
sections.summary: The second step of the GST increase could be paused should inflation be much higher than expected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Second, on pausing the second step of GST increase, should there be much higher than expected inflation.

sections.label: Reviewing second GST step
sections.summary: If that happened, they would pause to review economic circumstances and consider their position for the second step.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: If something like that were to happen, then as I said just now, we will certainly take a pause to review, to take stock of the economic circumstances and consider our position for the second step.

sections.label: No unspent revenue
sections.summary: Nowadays budgets are balanced or in deficit, so there is no unspent revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Maybe in the past but nowadays, what surplus are we talking about?

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We literally are running balanced Budgets, if not deficit Budgets, so there is no unspent revenue.

sections.label: HDB deficit financing
sections.summary: HDB has long been financed on its deficit, selling flats at subsidised prices below development cost.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: This has been going on for years since I was a young officer in MOF.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have always financed HDB on its deficit, it is called deficit financing, which means when HDB has a deficit because it has a shortfall, it has to sell the flats at a subsidised price, the selling price is less than the development cost, deficit.

sections.label: Consolidated fund, no hypothecation
sections.summary: All Government funding sources go into a consolidated fund, and revenue is not hypothecated to specific spending.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The basic point is all Government sources of funding, whether from NIRC or from revenue, come into a consolidated fund.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We do not hypothecate, which is something that Mr Leong is saying – identify this revenue source, link to this particular spending item.

sections.label: Setting aside surplus into funds
sections.summary: With a surplus, the Government might set aside some into funds for longer-term needs, having set aside $5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Well, if there is that surplus, we might very well consider whether there are longer-term needs in the future that would be prudent for us to set aside some of that surplus into these so-called funds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have set aside, I think, $5 billion.

sections.label: Reserves size and policy evolution
sections.summary: A Member asks whether larger reserves warrant different policies, noting about $50 billion was drawn down during COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: But my clarification is really on whether the Deputy Prime Minister would acknowledge that as countries evolve, societies evolve, and also as the size, the absolute size of the financial reserves increase, different policies, are necessary and advisable, compared to when the reserves was $100 billion versus what it is now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: And on this point, in this context, I would like to bring Members back to the point my colleague, Mr Louis Chua, made that in the crisis of a generation, during COVID-19, many Members of this House, used the term "the crisis of our generation", "the crisis of our generation", we drew down about $50 billion.

sections.label: Disagreement over reserves use
sections.summary: The disagreement is stated as the Workers' Party wanting to use more past reserves and leave less for future generations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Lim was asking the Deputy Prime Minister whether healthcare expenditure, which is usually given as the main reason for increasing the GST, and that has seen a secular increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: First, Mr Leon Perera says there is a disagreement with philosophy and the main disagreement is on the slope of the growth in reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I would say the main disagreement is this: the Workers' Party basically wants to use more past reserves and leave behind less for our children and grandchildren – just state it honestly.

sections.label: Forefathers' NIRC approach counterfactual
sections.summary: If forefathers had taken 20% more NIRC, today's GST would be 11% instead of 9%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Is it wise to do it this way?

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And if you think about it, if our forefathers had taken that same approach, I said in my Budget speech or in my round-up speech during the debate, if our forefathers had thought exactly the same line of thought, take 20% more of NIRC for themselves, today, we will be not just talking about a 9% GST, we will be talking about an 11% GST.

sections.label: Past reserves use and system
sections.summary: The Government's position is not to change the parameters of today's system now, given possible future emergencies requiring past reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: How can one tell whether or not in the coming years there will not be similar emergencies, pandemics, crises for which we may very well legitimately have to go to the President and ask for permission to use the past reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, in light of all of these considerations, I would say, the Government's position is very much to say today's system, do not change the parameters now.

sections.label: Nearer-term projections and increase trend
sections.summary: Nearer-term projections may be lumpy and unpredictable, but the broader trend of increase is clear and preparation should start now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, these are nearer-term projections which may be slightly lumpy, a little bit more unpredictable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But the broader trend of increase is very clear and we have start preparing now for that increase.

sections.label: Workers' Party records dissent
sections.summary: The Workers' Party records its dissent, and Members wishing to dissent are asked to rise to their feet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The Workers' Party would like to record our dissent, please.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Would you like to call for a Division or would you like to record your dissent instead?

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Would Members who wish to dissent, please rise to your feet.
